summary: Long Beach operates its own port — the second-busiest container port in the Western Hemisphere — which means a city of 460,000 residents sits at the nexus of a massive global logistics engine, generating thousands of jobs in shipping, warehousing, and trade services without residents needing to commute to downtown Los Angeles. That economic base is supplemented by a sizable healthcare sector, aerospace and defense employers (Boeing's C-17 program was assembled here for decades), and a Cal State university campus enrolling tens of thousands of students, so switching employers without leaving the city is genuinely plausible. The terrain is mostly flat coastal plain, and the beachfront stretches for miles, but the view seaward includes oil islands — artificial platforms camouflaged with decorative structures since the 1960s — a detail that surprises newcomers expecting an unbroken Pacific horizon. At a median household income of roughly $84,000 and a median home price above $762,000, the price-to-income ratio lands around 9:1, pushing homeownership out of comfortable reach at the median and keeping median rent near $1,800. Daily highs averaging 73°F with over nine hours of sunshine make the climate genuinely mild year-round, and the city's grid of bike paths, a waterfront pedestrian trail, and a light-rail line connecting to LA give it more transit bones than most Southern California cities its size. Long Beach is a working port city that happens to have a boardwalk — and the tension between industrial grit and coastal leisure defines nearly every block.
